texts.preamble: John P. Stephen vs Food Inspector on 27 January, 2016 Author: B.Sudheendra Kumar Bench: B.Sudheendra Kumar In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present: The Honourable Mr. Justice B.Sudheendra Kumar Wednesday, The 27Th Day Of January 2016/7Th Magha, 1937 Crl.Rev.Pet.No. 435 of 2007 ( ) -------------------------------- Crl.A 195/2006 Of The Additional Sessions Court/Spl. Court (Ndps Act Cases), Thodupuzha In Cc 163/2004 Of The Chief Judicial Magistrate Court, Thodupuzha Revision Petitioner(S)/Appellant/2Nd Accused: -------------------------------------------- John P. Stephen, S/O. Ouseph Stephen, Pulimoottil House, Thodupuzha. By Adv. Sri.K.A.Salil Narayanan Respondents/Respondents/Complainant & State: ---------------------------------------------- 1. Food Inspector, Muvattupuzha Municipality. (In Charge Of Thodupuzha Municipality.) 2. State Of Kerala, Represented By Public Prosecutor, High Court Of Kerala, Ernakulam. By Public Prosecutor Sri.V.S.Sreejith This Criminal Revision Petition Having Been Finally Heard On 27-01-2016, Along With Crrp. 438/2007, The Court On The Same Day Passed The Following: John P. Stephen vs Food Inspector on 27 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/159098095/ 1 Scl. B. Sudheendra Kumar, J. ------------------------------------- Crl.R.P. Nos. 435 & 438 of 2007 -------------------------------------- Dated this the 27th day of January, 2016 Order
texts.facts: The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 24.2.2000 at about 2.30 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 600 gram of banana chips from the first accused. The second accused was the licencee of the said shop. After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis. The Public Analyst filed Ext.P13 report stating that the sample contained added synthetic colouring matter tartrazine and was therefore adulterated. Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample Crl.R.P. 435 & 438 of 2007 2 was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext .P16 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would show that the sample of banana chips contained water soluble synthetic colour in violation of Rule 29 of P.F.A. Rules, 1955. It was further reported in Ext.P16 certificate that the sample did not contain proper label declaration as required under Rule 32 of the P.F.A. Rules, 1955 and hence the sample was adulterated as well as misbranded. 4. Before the trial court, PW1 and PW2 were examined and Exts.P1 to P23 were marked for the prosecution. DW1 and DW2 were examined on the side of the revision petitioner. 5. The learned advocates for the revision petitioners have argued that the materials on record would show that the sample forwarded to the Central Food Laboratory was only one of the three samples prepared by PW1 after the purchase of the food item from the shop of the second accused and hence, the finding by the Central Food Laboratory that the Crl.R.P. 435 & 438 of 2007 3 sample did not contain proper label declaration cannot be correct. Ext.P6 mahazar would show that the food inspector purchased 600 gram of banana chips and thereafter, he divided the same into three parts John P. Stephen vs Food Inspector on 27 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/159098095/ 2 and each part was put in different packets and thereafter, the said packets were sealed. During the course of evidence, PW1 stated that since the food item purchased did not contain the label, PW1 opened the packets and put the food item in a clean paper and mixed. Thereafter, it was divided into three parts and each part was packed in separate polythene packets and one of the said packets was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. It is clear from the evidence of PW1 that the sample analysed in the Central Food Laboratory was the sample prepared by PW1 as stated above.
texts.arguments: 6. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis Crl.R.P. 435 & 438 of 2007 5 was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P16 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on Crl.R.P. 435 & 438 of 2007 6 such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused. The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioners and the learned Public Prosecutor.

The learned counsel for the revision petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioners and the learned Public Prosecutor.
